interactive.title: Two brackets as an area
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in thirteen small screens on a rectangle. Its width is one bracket and its height is the other, so its area is the two brackets multiplied. Each side is cut at a split into an x part and a number part, and lines from the two splits cut the rectangle into four tiles. The x by x tile is a square, x², the two strips are x times each number, and the small corner is the two numbers multiplied. Each tile shows its name and, when x has a value, its area. The tiles added up give the expanded rule underneath, with the two strips collected into one term. A slider for x stretches every x part together, and dragging the split on a side changes that side's number, so the strips, the corner and the rule all change with it. When both sides are the same the rectangle is a square and its two strips match. A side such as 2x + 1 has two x parts, so it makes two x² tiles. Where a bracket has a minus sign the rectangle becomes a grid, with one bracket's terms across the top and the other's down the side, and each cell holds those two terms multiplied, with its sign. A cell below zero is hatched, because no tile can have an area below zero. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. A puzzle offers three answers, and a wrong pick is checked by putting a number into the brackets and into that answer, which come out different.
interactive.ignores: The rectangle draws x as one positive length. On the first screen the tiles are to scale for the x on the slider; on the other rectangle screens x is drawn at a length that matches no whole number, and the picture says it is not to scale. x can be any number, negative or a fraction, and every expansion here still holds. The grid's hatched cells are terms below zero, not areas. The numbers in the brackets and the puzzles are small whole numbers chosen as examples, so the tiles can be drawn and counted.

explain.text:
Multiplying two brackets can be pictured as finding the area of a rectangle whose sides are the two brackets. Picture a rectangle x + 3 wide and x + 2 tall.[^1] Cut each side where its x part ends and its number part begins, and lines from those splits cut the rectangle into four tiles. x by x is x², x by 2 is 2x, 3 by x is 3x and 3 by 2 is 6. The area can be written as the two brackets multiplied or as the four tiles added, and these are two ways of writing the same area, so they are equal.[^2] Writing it as the tiles added is expanding the brackets, as in Linear equations. Collect the two strips, 3x + 2x = 5x, and (x + 3)(x + 2) = x² + 5x + 6. At x = 4 the brackets make 7 × 6 = 42, and the tiles make 16 + 12 + 8 + 6 = 42.

Drag the splits to other numbers a and b and the tiles keep the same pattern. The strips are ax and bx, which add to (a + b)x, and the corner is a × b, so (x + a)(x + b) = x² + (a + b)x + ab. A two-term bracket such as x + a is called a [[binomial]],[^3] and an expression like this, whose highest power of x is x², is a [[quadratic]].[^4] When both sides are x + 5 the rectangle is a square, and its two strips are both 5x, so (x + 5)² = x² + 10x + 25. An easy slip is to write x² + 25, which leaves out both strips. With numbers, (1 + 4)² = 25, but 1² + 4² is only 17. The missing 8 is the two strips, 1 × 4 and 4 × 1. In letters, (x + y)² = x² + 2xy + y², and the 2xy is those two strips.

A tile cannot have an area below zero, so a term like −4 has no tile, and the rectangle becomes a grid. The grid still gives the right answer, because it needs no lengths, only the single bracket of Linear equations used twice: (x − 4)(x + 1) = x(x + 1) − 4(x + 1) = x² + x − 4x − 4. Each cell takes its sign from the signs rule of Negative numbers, so −4 × x is −4x and −4 × 1 is −4. The four cells collect to x² − 3x − 4. At x = 5 the brackets make 1 × 6 = 6, and 25 − 15 − 4 = 6. In (x + 3)(x − 3) the two x cells are 3x and −3x, which cancel, leaving x² − 9. A number in front of x works the same way, as 2x × x is 2x², so (2x + 1)(x + 3) = 2x² + 6x + x + 3 = 2x² + 7x + 3.

In the course puzzle, the load's power turns out to be a rule with the current squared in it, and later lessons find its peak by rewriting such rules between bracket form and expanded form, of which expanding is the first. **Two brackets multiply as the four tiles of a rectangle with those sides, every term in the first times every term in the second,[^5] so (x + 3)(x + 2) = x² + 5x + 6.**

analogy.text: Say a plant room's floor is 4 m by 3 m, and you extend it 1 m one way and 2 m the other. The new floor is (4 + 1) × (3 + 2) = 25 m². That is the old 12 m², a strip of 4 × 2 = 8 m², a strip of 1 × 3 = 3 m² and a corner of 1 × 2 = 2 m², the same four tiles. Forget the corner and you order 2 m² of flooring too little.
analogy.breaks: A floor's sides are positive lengths, so it cannot show a minus sign in a bracket, which needs the grid. A floor also has one fixed size, while in algebra x can be any number and the expansion holds for all of them.

practice.text:
- Multiply every term in the first bracket by every term in the second.[^5] Two brackets of two terms give four products.
- Give each product its sign, as in Negative numbers.
- Collect like terms, usually the two middle ones.
- Try a number in the brackets and in your answer, then a second number.

**Rule of thumb:** For (x + a)(x + b), the middle number is a + b and the end number is a × b. A squared bracket has two equal strips, so (x + a)² = x² + 2ax + a².

**Worked example:** (x − 3)(2x + 5). The four products are x × 2x = 2x², x × 5 = 5x, −3 × 2x = −6x and −3 × 5 = −15. The middle two collect to 5x − 6x = −x, so the answer is 2x² − x − 15. As a check, at x = 4 the brackets make 1 × 13 = 13, and 32 − 4 − 15 = 13.

**Common mistakes**
- Leaving out the strips, so (x + 5)² becomes x² + 25. With numbers, (1 + 4)² is 25 but 1² + 4² is only 17.
- Adding the two numbers for the end term, so (x + 4)(x + 1) ends + 5. They multiply, giving + 4.
- Losing a sign, so (x + 5)(x − 2) ends + 10. +5 × −2 is −10, so it is x² + 3x − 10. Try x = 3, which gives 8 against 28.
- Dropping the number in front, so (2x + 1)(x + 3) starts x². 2x × x is 2x².

interactive.html:
A rectangle whose sides are two brackets, cut into tiles, then a grid for brackets with a minus sign. Every number tried is an example.

Each tile or cell is one term of the first bracket times one term of the second.
interactive.title: Two brackets as an area
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is a rectangle with sides x + a and x + b cutting into four tiles, x², ax, bx and ab, that add up to the expanded rule, when you drag the split on each side.

checks.label: When expanding double brackets, every term in the first bracket is multiplied by every term in the second: on every screen the tiles or cells drawn are those products, they add up to the answer, and the brackets and the answer make the same value at every number tried, whole, a half or negative
A rectangle whose height is x + 2 and width is x + 3 opens the lesson, drawn to scale at every x on the slider

The brackets multiplied and the tiles added are two ways of expressing the same area, so they are equal: at every x on the slider the tiles drawn fill the rectangle exactly, each to scale for its area, and both lines of working make the same value

Every worked number is right (42 and 16 + 12 + 8 + 6 at x = 4; 18, 8 and 19; 18 at x = 1; 40, 49 and 31; 36 and 26; 25, 13, 19 and 22; 6 at x = 5; 8, 28 and −10; 16; 15, 113 and 127; 12; 5, 7 and −2; 16, 40 and −56), and every line of working on every screen adds up
Each puzzle accepts only the expansion of its brackets, and every wrong answer offered is marked as a slip making a different value at the number tried
Before an answer, a puzzle's picture names no tile or cell and shows no answer row
A cell is hatched exactly when its term is below zero: −4x and −4 in (x − 4)(x + 1), while in (x − 6)² the corner −6 × −6 makes 36 and is not

Dragging the sides: for every pair of numbers from 1 to 6 the strips are each number times x, the corner is the two numbers multiplied, the rule collects them, and at x = 1 the brackets and the tiles make the same value
A square has two equal strips: (x + 5)² has two strips of 5x, the 10x that x² + 25 leaves out; and in (x + 3)(x − 3) and (x + 7)(x − 7) the two x cells cancel, leaving no x term
Every demonstration has finished arriving within 4.5 s of its screen opening, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; every answer's motion, right or wrong, within 2.5 s

applied.problem: The opening states as a general fact that multiplying brackets is finding an area, which fails once a bracket has a minus sign (the lesson itself later says no tile can be negative); and the splits only drag from 1 to 6, not to any numbers.
